Museo del Prado. Spain's national art museum in Madrid, the Prado opened in 1819 and showcases the finest Spanish paintings alongside works collected by Spanish royalty across centuries. Its unparalleled holdings of Velázquez, Goya, and Bosch make it indispensable for understanding European painting. Founded by Ferdinand the Seventh to house the Spanish royal collection, the museum occupies a Neoclassical building by Juan de Villanueva that remains an architectural icon. The collection's centerpiece is Velázquez's Las Meninas, arguably the most influential painting in Western art. This work is surrounded by his royal portraits and court scenes, all documenting the height of Spanish royal patronage. The museum also contains Goya's Black Paintings, searing murals transferred from his own house, which revolutionized Romantic and modern aesthetics through their psychological intensity and dark vision. Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights is the world's most significant holding of the fifteenth-century master's visionary and deeply enigmatic works. The Prado is strong in Spanish Gothic, Mannerist, and Baroque painting, and it also holds significant holdings of Flemish and Italian masters that were purchased by Spanish kings during their periods of European dominance. The building's triple-tiered architecture was innovative for its time. In 2007, Rafael Moneo added modern gallery space through careful expansion that preserved the original structure's dominance. Together, these holdings make the Prado the canonical resource for tracing Spain's artistic tradition from the Romanesque period onward, and Las Meninas remains a turning point in art history.
